stem: A post-stroke client has confirmed oropharyngeal dysphagia and is cleared for a modified oral diet. Which nursing plan best reduces swallowing-related risk?

options.A: Follow the individualized swallowing plan for posture/positioning, food texture and liquid consistency, pacing, cueing, and supervision during oral intake, and reassess if swallowing status changes.
options.B: Use the same thickened-liquid level and chin-tuck position for every client with post-stroke dysphagia regardless of the swallowing evaluation.
options.C: Encourage rapid eating so the meal is completed before fatigue develops, even if the client coughs or requires repeated swallows.
options.D: Assume texture modification eliminates aspiration risk, so ongoing observation and reassessment are unnecessary once the diet order is written.

rationale: A is correct. ASHA guidance emphasizes individualized dysphagia management based on swallowing assessment, including posture/positioning, compensatory strategies, bolus or diet-texture modification, pacing/cueing, and patient/caregiver education. Texture-modified foods and thickened liquids do not eliminate aspiration or pneumonia risk, and reassessment may be needed when clinical status changes. B applies one strategy to every patient even though postural and consistency recommendations depend on swallowing physiology. C may increase risk when fatigue, impulsivity, coughing, or multiple swallows are present. D incorrectly treats diet modification as a guarantee of airway protection.
educational_objective: Implement post-stroke dysphagia precautions according to the individualized swallowing evaluation—using appropriate positioning, texture/viscosity, pacing, cueing, and supervision—and continue monitoring because modified diets do not eliminate aspiration risk.
source_organization: American Speech-Language-Hearing Association (ASHA); American Heart Association / American Stroke Association
source_document_title: Adult Dysphagia Practice Portal; 2026 Guideline for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke
source_version_date: ASHA current Practice Portal accessed 2026-08-17; AHA/ASA guideline published January 26, 2026
source_locator: ASHA Adult Dysphagia — intervention may include compensatory swallowing strategies, posture considerations, bolus consistency modification, pacing/cueing, education, and reassessment; Diet Texture Modifications: texture/thickened-liquid changes must be individualized and may not eliminate aspiration or pneumonia risk. AHA/ASA 2026 Section 5.2 Dysphagia: swallowing evaluation and management should identify at-risk patients and guide appropriate oral/nutritional management, while aspiration risk can persist despite screening or restrictions.
source_claim_supported: For a stroke patient with confirmed dysphagia who is permitted oral intake, aspiration-risk reduction requires individualized swallowing strategies and diet/positioning recommendations with ongoing monitoring; no single posture or consistency is appropriate for all patients and modification does not eliminate aspiration risk.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing
blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity — Reduction of Risk Potential: implement interventions based on identified aspiration risk, monitor response to treatment plans, and recognize changes requiring reassessment.
blueprint_topic: Reduction of Risk Potential — individualized aspiration precautions for post-stroke dysphagia
correction_summary: Rebuilt the raw generic aspiration-precaution list to remove the unsupported universal rule of 'upright during and after meals' and the implication that every dysphagic patient needs the same modified consistency or supervision level. The final item uses individualized swallowing-plan elements supported by ASHA and preserves the limitation that texture modification does not eliminate aspiration risk.
audit_reviewer: OpenAI GPT-5.6 Sol — Rule 1 clinical audit + adversarial second pass

audit_findings.source_audit: Verified against current ASHA Adult Dysphagia guidance and the 2026 AHA/ASA stroke dysphagia section.
audit_findings.claim_by_claim: A reflects individualized assessment-based management. B imposes universal posture/consistency strategies. C disregards fatigue and airway-warning signs. D falsely assumes modified consistency removes aspiration risk.
audit_findings.choice_A: Correct; follow individualized posture, consistency, pacing and supervision recommendations.
audit_findings.choice_B: Incorrect; swallowing strategies are physiology- and patient-specific.
audit_findings.choice_C: Incorrect; rapid intake may worsen safety and ignores clinical signs.
audit_findings.choice_D: Incorrect; aspiration can still occur on modified diets.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only A avoids prescribing a universal posture or liquid thickness and correctly preserves the need for reassessment.
audit_findings.cueing: All options address oral-feeding management for confirmed dysphagia.
audit_findings.blueprint: Aspiration-risk management and monitoring fit Reduction of Risk Potential.
audit_findings.independent_adversarial_second_pass: Rechecked posture, chin-tuck variability, texture-modification limitations, pacing, supervision and reassessment. Removed unsupported fixed positioning duration and found no second defensible answer.
